## Abstract

After a period of relative continuity, environmental and climate policymaking has experienced considerable turbulence over the past decade. In a time increasingly perceived as crisis-ridden, climate change and other global environmental issues have become subjects of heated debate and societal conflicts. At the same time, there are efforts to counteract these dynamics by stripping environmental and climate issues of their political character and delegating them to experts. The contributions to the Research Topic “(De-)Politicizing Climate and Environmental Politics in Times of Crisis: Contexts, Strategies, and Effects” are based on the shared presumption that the concepts of “politicization” and “depoliticization” offer useful analytical lenses through which to understand and decipher these current dynamics. This introductory article to the Research Topic systematizes key understandings of (de)politicization and proposes a heuristic framework based on six key questions: Who (de)politicizes what, how, when, where, and with what effect? The framework serves to provide a structured overview of the diversity of current (de)politicization phenomena in environmental and climate policy, as detailed in the contributions to the Research Topic. Across the contributions, it becomes apparent how differently processes of (de)politicization shape the possibilities and limitations of environmental and climate policy, as well as their democratic legitimation.

## 1 Introduction

Current climate and environmental governance spans across a wide range of policy domains, such as water, mobility, energy, food and agriculture. This multi-sectoral scope gives rise to numerous lines of conflict, driven by a variety of actors and their different interests, perspectives and knowledge repertoires. Discourses around (global) environmental issues have become increasingly polarized, contributing to intensified political divides and divergent public beliefs, among others, about the nature and urgency of climate change (Chinn et al., 2020) and how governing the climate crisis affects individual lifestyles, identities, and communities (Wendler, 2022). These tensions position environmental and climate governance as complex fields of research and action that must take into account not only the institutional dimensions of politics but also temporal, geographical, material, ethical, moral, and cultural aspects.

Since the adoption of the Paris Agreement in 2015 and a call for “all hands on deck” (Hale, 2016) in a collaborative governance setting (Marquardt et al., 2022), climate governance has been characterized by a steady rise in political contestation. The assumption that global commitments under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), along with existing technical expertise, market-based solutions and narratives of shared gains for all parties, could depoliticize climate action has been increasingly challenged. Technocratic solutions appear insufficient to keep global warming within the 1.5 °C threshold (WMO, 2024), while mitigation and adaptation measures are entangled in distributional conflicts, societal divisions and policy backlash (Marquardt and Lederer, 2022; Patterson, 2023). Climate change has become a mobilizing issue not only for populist parties and (radical) social movements, but for a diversity of actors, from companies facing the impacts of climate legislation to coal-dependent communities that feel marginalized by the transition. They engage with climate change either by promoting denialism, skepticism, and a defense of a fossil-fueled, growth-oriented development model, or by invoking emotions, highlighting injustices, and resorting to civil disobedience.

While some scholars view these tensions and political conflicts over climate change as a potential threat to effective policy (Kahan, 2012; Nisbet and Fahy, 2015), others contend that decades of framing climate change as a scientific and technocratic issue have suppressed vital political questions and sidelined democratic deliberation. These critics call for open political debates on climate change to surface marginalized perspectives and challenge dominant imaginaries of sustainable development (Machin, 2015; Swyngedouw, 2022). Hence, the politics of climate change and its (de-)politicization have unfolded along parallel and often contradictory dynamics. How can we make sense of these fragmented, differentiated and conflicting trends?

Despite its analytical promise, (de-)politicization remains an underexplored and weakly systematized entry point for capturing the wide range of dynamics addressed in this Research Topic. Existing scholarship employs the concept in divergent and often implicit ways, resulting in conceptual ambiguity and limited comparability across studies. Against this backdrop, this contribution addresses the lack of a shared understanding of what (de-)politicization entails and how it can be studied by advancing a framework to guide related research. The framework specifies six core dimensions of (de-)politicization, structured around the guiding questions of who politicizes what, how, when, where, and with what effects. Rather than proposing operationalizable indicators, the framework is deliberately heuristic: it provides a structured set of analytical questions that enable systematic and critical engagement with heterogeneous processes of (de-)politicization across empirical contexts.

Politicization is defined here as a concept with two critical elements. First, politicization means that an issue or problem becomes the subject of intense public attention and debate. Politicization occurs when an issue moves from the realm of necessity and the private sphere into the public and, eventually, the governmental sphere. Second, politicization means that matters become “a site of ongoing contestation” (Brown, 2015, p. 4) and get exposed to “public debates about the right course in handling a given problem” (Zürn, 2014, p. 50). Highlighting contingency and contestation, politicization is thereby defined “as an increase in polarization of opinions, interests or values and the extent to which they are publicly advanced towards the process of policy formulation” (de Wilde, 2011, p. 572).

In contrast, depoliticization is defined here as the avoidance or silencing of controversies, often through professionalization, technicization, and the delegation of responsibilities to administrative bodies, thereby excluding these measures from the political sphere (Feindt et al., 2021, pp. 4–5). Issues thereby move from the public to the private sphere, shifting from contestation to necessity and transferring control from government to external agencies, science, and bureaucracy. Governments attempt to depoliticize issues by removing them from the political agenda, delegating them to other actors, and framing them in ways that leave no alternative to a particular political decision (Wood and Flinders, 2014). The resulting post-political condition is a consensus built on scientific evidence, rational truth, and undeniable facts (Crouch, 2004; Pepermans and Maeseele, 2016, p. 480; Swyngedouw, 2011).

Politicization is not historically unprecedented. In fact, environmental policy has always been contested, with different groups and actors aiming to shape public discourse and policymaking in domestic and international contexts. Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring (Carson, 1962), for example, sparked widespread public outrage over pesticide use in the United States, helping to ignite the modern environmental movement while provoking fierce backlash from the chemical industry and its political allies. The 1972 United Nations Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm brought ecological concerns onto the global political agenda, but also exposed early tensions between different development models, fueling fears that environmental regulation might impede economic development. Also, interest groups, such as the fossil fuel industry, have long engaged in lobbying and political campaigns to influence environmental policy and hinder progress in global environmental governance. Hence, over the past decades, ecological debates have not only addressed environmental issues but also exposed underlying normative tensions and competing ideas about how societies should be organized more broadly (Marquardt and Schoppek, 2023).

Politicization is thus a double-edged sword: on the one hand, it can mobilize the public, drive policy change, and foster the collective action needed to address pressing issues such as climate change and biodiversity loss. On the other hand, it can also lead to polarization, provoke resistance as well as backlash, and entrench opposing positions, potentially stalling progress. The same applies to depoliticization: while often criticized as a means of maintaining established–and frequently unsustainable—conditions by suppressing dissent, it can also serve as a tool for resolving conflicts and restoring collective agency following periods of intense political confrontation.

To examine the multifaceted dynamics of (de-)politicization, this introduction will explore both their transformative potential and pitfalls, recognizing the constructive and constraining effects they may have on environmental and climate governance. First, we examine how different bodies of literature use the concepts of politicization and depoliticization (Section 2). We then propose a heuristic framework composed of six core dimensions for analyzing (de-)politicization (Section 3), before introducing the contributions to this Research Topic, highlighting how each engages with one or more of these dimensions (Section 4). Finally, we identify overarching themes that emerge from the contributions to this Research Topic and outline avenues for future research (Section 5).

## 2 Conceptualizing (de-)politicization

The concepts “politicization” and “depoliticization” are widely used across fields like Public Administration (Hustedt and Salomonsen, 2014; Peters and Pierre, 2025), International Relations (Rauh and Zürn, 2020), and European Studies (Hackenesch et al., 2021; Zeitlin et al., 2019). However, no generally accepted definitions exist. Instead, (de-)politicization constitute “essentially contested concepts” (Gallie, 1956), characterized by rival interpretations and ongoing debates over its meaning and application, thus mirroring the dynamics of real-world politicization in practice. These divergent conceptualizations reflect differing worldviews, epistemological positions, and analytical perspectives. Generally speaking, politicization refers to processes through which actors become aware of their interests and identities and articulate them collectively in the broader public sphere, thereby asserting claims to broader social or political legitimacy (Mouffe, 2005; Zürn, 2014).
